nameStory: The American plum earned its name simply by being our continent's native plum species, distinguishing it from European plums brought by colonists. Early settlers also called it 'wild plum' since they found it growing untamed in thickets and woodland edges. Some knew it as 'Marshall's large yellow sweet plum' after someone who likely promoted a particularly tasty variety.
description: American plum is a small native tree or large shrub that typically grows 12-20 feet tall, often forming dense thickets through root sprouts. In spring, it puts on a spectacular white flower show before the leaves fully emerge, covering its branches like fresh snow. The small, round fruits ripen to bright red or yellow in late summer, about the size of large cherries. Its oval leaves have finely toothed edges and the bark is dark brown with shallow furrows.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round plums about 1 inch across that ripen to bright red or golden yellow in late summer. The skin feels smooth and has a slight waxy bloom, while the flesh is juicy but often quite tart, puckering your mouth if eaten unripe.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Clusters of pure white flowers with five rounded petals appear in early spring before leaves emerge. Each flower is about 1 inch across with many prominent yellow stamens in the center, and they have a sweet, pleasant fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 2-4 inches long with sharply pointed tips and finely serrated edges that feel slightly rough to the touch. They're arranged alternately on branches and turn yellow to orange in fall.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense thickets through underground root sprouts, creating colonies of multiple stems. Individual trees have a rounded crown with somewhat thorny, zigzagging branches.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Dark brown to grayish bark with shallow furrows and scaly plates. On younger branches, the bark is smoother and reddish-brown with prominent horizontal lines called lenticels.

habitat: American plum thrives in woodland edges, old fields, and along streams where it gets plenty of sunlight but some protection from harsh winds. It prefers well-drained soils and often grows in thickets along fence rows, abandoned farmland, and the margins between forest and open areas. You'll most commonly spot it in disturbed areas where it can spread freely through root suckers.

seasonality.spring: Showy white flowers bloom in April to early May before leaves fully emerge, creating spectacular displays along woodland edges. The sweet fragrance attracts numerous bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Small green fruits develop and gradually ripen to red or yellow by late summer. Leaves are fully developed, showing their distinctive serrated edges and oval shape.
seasonality.fall: Ripe plums may persist into early fall, and leaves turn bright yellow to orange before dropping. This is prime harvest time for both wildlife and humans.
seasonality.winter: Bare thorny branches reveal the thicket-forming growth habit, with dark scaly bark and small, pointed buds visible along zigzagging twigs.

funFact: American plums are nature's ultimate collaborative fruit - the trees are largely self-sterile, meaning they need pollen from a genetically different American plum to produce fruit, which is why they evolved to form those dense thickets where multiple genetic individuals can cross-pollinate each other.
confusionNotes: American plum is most easily confused with Canada plum, but American plum fruits are smaller, rounder, and ripen to bright red rather than yellow. Beach plum grows in coastal areas and has much smaller, duller leaves, while wild cherries have longer, more pointed leaves and dark purple fruits in drooping clusters rather than individual plums.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'wild plum,' American plum has been cultivated by Indigenous peoples for centuries and many domestic plum varieties were developed from this species. It also serves as excellent rootstock for grafting European plums, combining hardiness with the superior fruit quality of domestic varieties.
compareHints: Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side. Compared to beach plum, American plum grows much larger, has bigger leaves, and forms inland thickets rather than coastal shrublands. The flowers of American plum are also larger and more showy than most of its Prunus relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
